# Why Is Nigeria on the Red List?

**By :** [Segun Dukeh](https://guardian.ng/author/sduqueguardian-ng/)

**Date:**  14 October 2026 12:34am WAT

**Share :**

[![](https://cdn.guardian.ng/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/google-1.png)Follow Us on Google Discover](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=The%20Guardian%20Nigeria%20News)

 ![nigeria-red-list-us-travel-ban-nigerian-passengers](https://cdn.guardian.ng/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/nigeria-red-list-us-travel-ban-nigerian-passengers.png) 

Welcome, and thank you for stopping by. If you have typed “why is Nigeria on the red list” into your phone this week, perhaps after somebody mentioned [a revived American entry ban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Trump_travel_ban) at a naming ceremony, you are in very good company. It is the question I hear most often this year, at weddings, in church car parks and in every family WhatsApp group that has ever forwarded a blurry screenshot at midnight. This article is the conclusion of months of research into travel and migration restrictions, and of years of experience helping Nigerians plan study, work and family trips abroad.

So let me start with the thing almost nobody explains.

There is no single red list. When Nigerians say “the red list” in 2026, they usually mean one of four quite different things: the United States travel ban that has partially restricted Nigerian visas since 1 January, the British list of countries whose health workers recruiters may not actively target, the American “Do Not Travel” warnings that cover 23 of our 36 states, or (for the older crowd) the hotel-quarantine list Britain used during the Omicron scare of December 2021. Each list is kept by a different government, for different reasons, with very different consequences for your wallet and your plans.

My cousin Funmi, a theatre nurse at a teaching hospital in Ibadan, rang me in February convinced she could no longer work in England “because Nigeria is on the red list”. Ten minutes later, her neighbour’s son in Yaba sent me a voice note, equally convinced he could still get a US student visa “because the red list is only for nurses”. They were both wrong, and both partly right, which is exactly why this topic deserves more than a headline.

Advertisement

By the end of this guide you will know which lists Nigeria is actually on in October 2026, which ones it has left, why each government says it put us there, and what you can practically do about it. I have converted costs at roughly ₦1,330 to the dollar, the official market rate in early October, so please refresh the figures if you are reading this months from now.

## Is Nigeria Still on the US Ban List in 2026?

Yes. As of mid-October 2026, Nigeria remains under partial restrictions.

[![EFN Non Oil Export](https://cdn.guardian.ng/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/WhatsApp-Image-2026-09-22-at-3.28.34-PM.jpeg)](https://exportfromnigeria.info/)

The instrument is Presidential Proclamation 10998, signed on 16 December 2025 and in force from 12:01am Eastern time on 1 January 2026. It placed Nigeria in the “partial” group, which suspends new immigrant visas (green cards for family and employment migration) and the B-1/B-2 visitor, F and M student and J exchange visas. Those happen to be the categories most Nigerian families actually use, so the word “partial” can feel a little generous.

What it does not do matters just as much. Visas issued before 1 January 2026 were not revoked, green card holders can still travel, and petition-based work visas such as the H-1B, L-1 and O-1 remain available, subject to heavier vetting. Nigerians may still pay for and attend visa interviews in suspended categories, but the US Mission has warned that they may be found ineligible for issuance. That is rather like being invited to sit an exam you have already been told you cannot pass.

Advertisement

Is this the first time? Not at all. In January 2020, an earlier proclamation suspended immigrant visas for Nigerians, a restriction reversed on 20 January 2021. Then in July 2025, Washington cut most non-immigrant visas for Nigerians to three months and a single entry, citing reciprocity. The foreign ministry responded through its spokesperson, Kimiebi Ebienfa, and [its formal request that Washington reconsider](https://von.gov.ng/nigeria-urges-us-to-reconsider-new-visa-restrictions/) described the move as out of step with the reciprocity and mutual respect expected between friendly nations. Five months later, the proclamation arrived anyway.

There is also a good deal of confusion about court rulings, so let me untangle it. On 21 August 2026, a federal judge in Manhattan voided a separate State Department pause on immigrant visas for 75 countries, and several Nigerian outlets reported it as the end of the ban. It was not. That ruling removed one extra layer, while Proclamation 10998 stayed exactly where it was (rather like clearing the go-slow on Third Mainland Bridge only to find the toll gate still shut).

The proclamation is reviewed every 180 days. The first review fell due in mid-June 2026 and Nigeria’s status did not change. The next falls due around mid-December, and the US Mission in Nigeria has said publicly that restrictions are not permanent and can ease if security and identity-management concerns are addressed. Any change will appear as an official notice with an effective date, not as a forwarded message from “a source at the embassy”.

Two further practical changes have tightened the squeeze. Since 1 August 2026, routine US visa services for Nigerians have been handled only at the Consulate General in Lagos, so an applicant from Maiduguri or Sokoto now has a very long journey for an interview. And a refundable visa bond of $10,000 to $20,000 (about ₦13.3 million to ₦26.6 million) can be demanded of otherwise eligible visitors.

Before any trip, anywhere, it is worth starting with our own government’s guidance. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs keeps [an advisory page for citizens travelling abroad](https://foreignaffairs.gov.ng/travel-advisory/) that sets out the basics many people still miss, including at least six months of passport validity, the right visa or entry permit, health insurance and registering with the nearest Nigerian mission. Boring? Perhaps. But I have watched a family lose a ₦4 million holiday at Murtala Muhammed because a passport had five months left on it.

For a clear account of how the American decision fell across the continent, Olayide Soaga published [a country-by-country breakdown in this paper on New Year’s Day](https://guardian.ng/news/why-us-is-placing-travel-ban-on-nigeria-25-other-african-countries/), setting out the overstay figures Washington quoted for each African nation it restricted. It is the quickest way to see that Nigeria is one of many, not singled out alone.

## Which Countries Are on the Red List With Nigeria?

This depends, again, on which red list you mean. Let us take them in order of how much they affect ordinary Nigerians.

### The US travel ban list

Proclamation 10998 covers 39 countries. Nineteen face a full suspension of both immigrant and non-immigrant visas: Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Burma, Chad, the Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Haiti, Iran, Laos, Libya, Mali, Niger, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, plus anyone travelling on documents issued by the Palestinian Authority.

Twenty more, including Nigeria, face partial restrictions: Angola, Antigua and Barbuda, Benin, Burundi, Côte d’Ivoire, Cuba, Dominica, Gabon, The Gambia, Malawi, Mauritania, Nigeria, Senegal, Tanzania, Togo, Tonga, Turkmenistan (immigrant visas only), Venezuela, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

Count the African names and you reach 26 of the 39. Ghana, Kenya and South Africa are not on it, which is why so many Nigerian students are now quietly redirecting their applications to Accra-based programmes and Canadian colleges.

Advertisement

### The UK health and care recruitment red list

This is the list Funmi was worried about, and it is real. Britain’s Code of Practice for international recruitment of health and social care staff grades countries red, amber or green, and the red list follows the World Health Organization’s Health Workforce Support and Safeguards List 2023, which identified 55 countries whose health systems are too short-staffed to lose workers to aggressive recruitment. Nigeria is on it, as it was on the earlier 2020 list, alongside Ghana, Cameroon, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal and roughly fifty others, most of them in Africa.

Here is the part that matters for Funmi. The red list stops British employers and agencies from actively targeting Nigerian health workers, but it does not stop a nurse in Ibadan from applying directly to an NHS trust on her own initiative. That loophole is wide. In the year to March 2026, Nigeria was the second-largest source of internationally educated nurses and midwives joining the UK register, with 1,614 new joiners. As far back as 2023, Chukwuma Muanya and Nkechi Onyedika-Ugoeze reported on [the scale of the nurse exodus to Britain](https://guardian.ng/news/intl-body-decries-poaching-as-nigeria-loses-2998-nurses-to-uk/), with 2,998 Nigerian-trained nurses lost to the NHS in a single year.

### Lists Nigeria has left

Not every list is bad news. In February 2023, the Financial Action Task Force placed Nigeria on its “grey list” of countries under increased monitoring for money laundering and terrorist financing. After a 19-point action plan, Nigeria was removed on 24 October 2025, and [the Presidency’s statement welcoming the delisting](https://statehouse.gov.ng/president-tinubu-welcomes-the-delisting-of-nigeria-from-the-fatf-grey-list-says-nigeria-is-committed-to-global-financial-transparency/) called it a milestone for financial credibility. The European Union followed by removing Nigeria from its list of high-risk third countries with effect from 29 January 2026.

Why should a trader in Onitsha care? Because grey-listing adds friction to every international payment, from importing spare parts to paying a child’s school fees abroad. Collins Olayinka’s analysis of [what the exit means for banks and businesses](https://guardian.ng/business-services/appraising-nigerias-exit-journey-from-fatf-grey-list/) explains why correspondent banks had been treating Nigerian transactions with extra suspicion, and why staying off the list requires the reforms to continue.

And the original “red list”? In December 2021, Britain added Nigeria to its Covid-19 travel red list during the Omicron scare, forcing arrivals into hotel quarantine. It lasted about nine days, from 6 to 15 December, before Britain scrapped the list entirely. People still quote it, which tells you how long a frightening headline can outlive the policy behind it.

### Every Red List Nigeria Sits On (or Has Left) in October 2026

| List | Who keeps it | What it does | Nigeria’s status, October 2026 | Others on it | What it means for you |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| US Proclamation 10998 | White House and State Department | Suspends immigrant, B-1/B-2, F, M and J visas | Partial restriction since 1 January 2026, reviewed every 180 days | 38 other countries, 26 of them African | A new $185 (about ₦246,050) visitor application is unlikely to succeed |
| US travel advisory | State Department | Rates risk for American travellers | Level 3 overall, with 23 states at Level 4 | 23 countries are Level 4 nationwide | No legal effect on Nigerians, but shapes insurance, conferences and investment |
| UK health and care recruitment red list | UK Department of Health, using the WHO 2023 list | Bars active recruitment of health workers | Red since 2023 | Ghana, Cameroon, Benin and about 50 more | Agencies cannot target you, but direct applications are allowed |
| FATF grey list | Financial Action Task Force | Increased monitoring of money laundering controls | Removed on 24 October 2025 | South Africa, Mozambique and Burkina Faso left at the same time | Less friction on international transfers |
| EU high-risk third countries | European Commission | Enhanced due diligence by EU banks | Removed with effect from 29 January 2026 | Varies by review | Easier banking relationships with Europe |
| UK Covid-19 travel red list | UK government | Hotel quarantine on arrival | Listed 6 to 15 December 2021, list now scrapped | Ten southern African countries | No effect today |

The pattern is clear: the lists that still bite are about migration and security (America’s ban and Britain’s health-worker rules), while the financial blacklists that once raised the cost of doing business from Lagos have been cleared.

## Why Is Nigeria on the Red List? The Direct Answer

If you only read one paragraph of this article, make it this one.

Nigeria is on the red list most people mean, the United States travel ban list under Presidential Proclamation 10998, because the White House said two things about us in December 2025: that armed groups such as Boko Haram and the Islamic State operate freely in parts of the country, creating “substantial screening and vetting difficulties”, and that Nigerians overstayed their visas at rates the US considered too high, with a B-1/B-2 visitor overstay rate of 5.56 per cent and an F, M and J student and exchange overstay rate of 11.90 per cent in the Department of Homeland Security’s Fiscal Year 2024 Entry/Exit Overstay Report. Separately, Nigeria sits on Britain’s health-worker recruitment red list because the World Health Organization ranks our health workforce among the 55 most vulnerable in the world, and 23 Nigerian states carry American “Do Not Travel” warnings because of terrorism, kidnapping and unrest. Nigeria is no longer on the FATF grey list, which it left in October 2025.

The entities behind those decisions are worth knowing by name, because they are the ones whose announcements actually change things:

* The White House and State Department, which issue and review Proclamation 10998 every 180 days
* The Department of Homeland Security, whose annual overstay report supplies the percentages
* The World Health Organization and the UK Department of Health and Social Care, which set and apply the health-worker safeguards list
* The State Department’s travel advisory service, which grades each Nigerian state for American visitors

Now for the honest part. Are those reasons fair?

On overstays, the comparison is uncomfortable for Washington’s logic. Senegal, also restricted, had a lower visitor overstay rate than Nigeria at 4.30 per cent, while Benin’s student overstay rate was 36.77 per cent and The Gambia’s 38.79 per cent. Nigeria’s figures were neither the worst nor the best, which suggests the decision rested as much on security, deportation cooperation and diplomatic temperature as on arithmetic. The restrictions also followed weeks after Washington redesignated Nigeria a “Country of Particular Concern” on religious freedom, and some Nigerian reporting linked the earlier July 2025 visa cuts partly to disagreements over accepting deportees.

None of that will comfort a student whose admission letter is sitting unused in a drawer in Owerri. But it does tell you something useful. Overstay rates are percentages of a small group of travellers, and every Nigerian who travels, complies and returns on time pulls that figure down for everybody else. I have always told the students I advise that their passport is carrying more than their own name.

Short version? Security and overstays put us on the American list. Health-worker shortages put us on the British one.

## Why Are Parts of Nigeria on the Do Not Travel List?

The phrase “Do Not Travel” comes from the US State Department, which grades every country from Level 1 (exercise normal precautions) to Level 4 (do not travel). Nigeria as a whole sits at Level 3, “Reconsider Travel”, because of crime, terrorism, unrest, kidnapping and inconsistent health care. When Washington published its global list of Level 4 countries in July 2026, Nigeria was not among the 23 nations on it.

The problem lies at state level. On 8 April 2026, the State Department expanded its Level 4 warnings to 23 of our 36 states and authorised non-emergency staff and their families to leave the embassy in Abuja. The states fall into three groups:

* Borno, Jigawa, Kogi, Kwara, Niger, Plateau, Taraba, Yobe and northern Adamawa, for terrorism, crime and kidnapping
* Bauchi, Gombe, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Sokoto and Zamfara, for unrest, crime and kidnapping
* Abia, Anambra, Bayelsa, Delta, Enugu, Imo and Rivers (excluding Port Harcourt), for crime, kidnapping and armed gangs

Britain’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office takes a similar line, advising against all travel to parts of the north-east and north-west and against all but essential travel to a wider list.

Read that list again and you will notice it leaves out Lagos, Ogun, Oyo, Osun, Ekiti, Ondo, Edo, Cross River, Akwa Ibom, Ebonyi, Kebbi, Nasarawa, Benue and the Federal Capital Territory. That is not a clean bill of health (they all still sit under the national Level 3 warning), but it is a long way from “Nigeria is a war zone”.

So why should Nigerians care about advice written for Americans? Three reasons, all practical. First, foreign travel insurers often refuse cover for areas their government warns against, which affects diaspora Nigerians visiting home for weddings and burials. Second, international conferences, NGOs and investors use these maps when deciding where to hold events and open offices, and a Level 4 label on Kano or Enugu quietly costs those cities business. Third, the security reasoning behind the advisories overlaps with the security reasoning behind the visa ban, so the two lists tend to move together.

I learnt this the slightly embarrassing way. A friend in Peckham booked flights for her father’s 70th birthday in Enugu, only to discover after landing that her annual travel policy excluded Level 4 states entirely. Nothing went wrong, thank God, but she spent the whole week mentally pricing hospital bills in pounds. Ten minutes reading the advisory before booking would have spared her that.

## Are Nigerians Allowed to Travel to the USA Now?

Some are. Most new applicants are not.

If you already hold a US visa issued before 1 January 2026 with entries remaining, you can still travel, although admission is decided by a border officer on arrival. Green card holders, Nigerians with a second passport from an unrestricted country (British, Canadian or Irish, for example), diplomats on A and G visas, athletes travelling for major sporting events, and applicants for petition-based work visas such as the H-1B, L-1 and O-1 can also still go. Everybody else in a suspended category depends on a national interest exception, which is rare, discretionary and has no application form.

I covered the categories, fees and the August court ruling in much more depth in my guide to [are Nigerians allowed to travel to the USA](https://guardian.ng/nigerian/are-nigerians-allowed-to-travel-to-the-usa/), so here I want to focus on what to do if you are planning around the red list right now. Think of it rather like preparing for an inspection at work: the outcome is not entirely in your hands, but the paperwork certainly is.

1. Name the list that actually affects you before spending a kobo. A nurse eyeing Manchester faces the UK recruitment rules, a student eyeing Texas faces Proclamation 10998, and a London-based relative planning a burial in Owerri faces the travel advisory, so write your trip and the relevant list on one line and ignore the noise about the others.
2. Check every passport and visa in the house. Your Nigerian passport needs at least six months of validity beyond your planned return and at least two blank pages, and if you need a new one, the Nigeria Immigration Service currently charges ₦100,000 for a 32-page, five-year booklet and ₦200,000 for a 64-page, ten-year booklet when you apply at home.
3. If your US category is suspended and you hold no older visa, second passport or approved employer petition, keep your money. A $185 visitor application (about ₦246,050) is non-refundable, and a student also pays a $350 SEVIS fee (about ₦465,500), which is a painful sum to lose on a near-certain refusal.
4. If your category is open, prepare the photograph exactly. US visa photos must be 2 by 2 inches (51mm by 51mm), taken within the last six months against a plain white or off-white background, with your head measuring 25mm to 35mm from chin to crown, and no glasses.
5. Build a document folder that a consular officer can read in thirty seconds. Use an A4 clear-pocket display book with coloured tabs in a fixed order (identity documents in blue, financial evidence in green, employment or study letters in yellow, travel history in red), and keep originals behind copies, because a neat folder signals an organised, credible applicant.
6. Health workers aiming for Britain should apply directly to NHS trusts and private providers rather than paying agents who claim to “place” them. An agency that targets you in a red-list country is breaching the Code of Practice, and any recruiter worth trusting will appear on the NHS Employers ethical recruiter list, which takes two minutes to check.
7. Put the next review dates in your calendar and check official sources only. Proclamation 10998 is next due for review around mid-December 2026, so follow the State Department, the US Mission in Nigeria and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs directly, and treat any WhatsApp message announcing that “the ban has been lifted” without an effective date as rumour until proven otherwise.

One styling note that sounds trivial but is not: dress for a visa interview as you would for a job interview at a bank in Marina. A pressed shirt, plain colours and closed shoes will never get you a visa on their own, but they help the officer focus on your answers rather than your outfit, and in a two-minute conversation that is worth having on your side.

## Final Thoughts: Why Is Nigeria on the Red List?

When Funmi finally understood that the UK red list stops recruiters rather than nurses, she laughed with relief, then went quiet. Her real question had never been about the list. It was whether staying in Ibadan and leaving for England could both be reasonable choices, and the honest answer is that they can.

That is the shape of this whole subject. Nigeria is on the red list most people mean because Washington cited insecurity in parts of the country and visa overstays, and it sits on Britain’s health-worker list because our hospitals cannot afford to lose more nurses and doctors. Twenty-three states carry American “Do Not Travel” warnings, while Lagos, Abuja and much of the south-west do not. And Nigeria has already climbed off two financial blacklists in the past year, which is a reminder that these lists can and do change when the underlying problems are addressed.

None of these lists defines you as a traveller, a professional or a Nigerian. They define the conditions you are working within for now, and the people who come through best are those who read the actual rules, keep their documents spotless and refuse to make expensive decisions on the strength of a forwarded voice note.

* Identify which specific list affects your plan this month and read its official wording before paying any fee or agent.
* Check every passport, visa and second-nationality document in your household for validity, entries and expiry dates this week.
* Diarise the mid-December 2026 review of Proclamation 10998 and follow only official State Department and Nigerian government channels for updates.

## Related Articles

If your interest in the red list is really a question about safety at home, my earlier guide to [whether it is safe to visit Nigeria](https://guardian.ng/nigerian/is-it-safe-to-visit-nigeria/) walks through the destinations that welcome visitors with reasonable confidence, from Lagos and Abuja to Calabar, and explains how to read foreign travel advisories without panicking. It pairs naturally with the state-by-state picture above, especially if you have relatives abroad who keep cancelling trips home.

And because the American ban sits inside a much longer relationship, my piece asking [whether Nigeria is friendly to the US](https://guardian.ng/nigerian/is-nigeria-friendly-to-the-us/) steps back to look at trade, security cooperation and the diaspora that bind the two countries. It was written before the proclamation took effect, which makes it a useful baseline for judging how far relations have shifted since.

## Key Takeaways

* The red list most Nigerians mean is US Proclamation 10998, which has suspended new visitor, student, exchange and immigrant visas for most Nigerians since 1 January 2026, citing insecurity and overstay rates of 5.56 and 11.90 per cent.
* Nigeria is also on Britain’s health-worker recruitment red list, which bars agencies from targeting Nigerian nurses and doctors but still allows direct applications to UK employers.
* Nigeria left the FATF grey list in October 2025 and the EU high-risk list in January 2026, while 23 states remain on America’s Level 4 “Do Not Travel” list.

## Frequently Asked Questions: Why Is Nigeria on the Red List?

### Why is Nigeria on the red list?

Nigeria is on the US travel ban list under Proclamation 10998 because Washington cited armed groups such as Boko Haram and the Islamic State, which it says make screening difficult, and overstay rates of 5.56 per cent for visitor visas and 11.90 per cent for student and exchange visas. It is also on Britain’s health-worker recruitment red list because the World Health Organization rates Nigeria’s health workforce as dangerously short-staffed.

### Is Nigeria still on the US ban list?

Yes, Nigeria remains on the partial restriction list under Proclamation 10998 as of October 2026, with no change at the first 180-day review in June. New B-1/B-2, F, M, J and immigrant visas are suspended for most Nigerians, although visas issued before 1 January 2026 remain valid.

### Which countries are in the red list?

The US travel ban covers 39 countries, with 19 under a full ban, including Afghanistan, Chad, Mali, Niger and Sierra Leone, and 20 under partial restrictions, including Nigeria, Senegal, Benin, Tanzania and Zimbabwe. Britain’s health-worker red list is a separate group of about 54 countries, including Nigeria, Ghana and Cameroon.

### Why is Nigeria on the do not travel list?

Nigeria as a whole is at Level 3, “Reconsider Travel”, in US advice, but 23 states are at Level 4, “Do Not Travel”, because of terrorism, kidnapping, armed gangs and unrest. These include Borno, Yobe, Kaduna, Kano, Zamfara and Rivers outside Port Harcourt, while Lagos and Abuja are not on the Level 4 list.

### Are Nigerians allowed to travel to the USA now?

Nigerians with a valid US visa issued before 1 January 2026, green card holders, dual nationals on unrestricted passports, diplomats and petition-based workers such as H-1B applicants can still travel. Most new visitor, student and immigrant applicants are refused unless they receive a rare national interest exception.

### When will the US travel ban on Nigeria be reviewed?

Proclamation 10998 is reviewed every 180 days, and the next review falls due around mid-December 2026. Any change for Nigeria will be published by the State Department and the US Mission in Nigeria with a clear effective date.

### Is Nigeria on the UK red list?

Nigeria is on the UK’s red list for the international recruitment of health and social care workers, based on the WHO Health Workforce Support and Safeguards List 2023. Britain’s Covid-19 travel red list, which briefly included Nigeria in December 2021, no longer exists.

### Can Nigerian nurses still work in the UK if Nigeria is on the red list?

Yes, Nigerian nurses can still apply directly to UK employers on their own initiative, and Nigeria was the second-largest source of new international nurses on the UK register in the year to March 2026. What the red list forbids is recruitment agencies and employers actively targeting health workers who live in Nigeria.

### Is Nigeria still on the FATF grey list?

No, the Financial Action Task Force removed Nigeria from its grey list on 24 October 2025 after it completed a 19-point action plan. The European Union also removed Nigeria from its list of high-risk third countries with effect from 29 January 2026.

### Will my existing US visa still work?

A US visa issued before 1 January 2026 was not revoked by the proclamation and can still be used until it expires or its entries run out. A border officer still decides admission on arrival, so carry evidence of your purpose of travel and your ties to Nigeria.

### How much does a US visa application cost a Nigerian in 2026?

A visitor visa application costs $185, about ₦246,050 at ₦1,330 to the dollar, and student applicants also pay a $350 SEVIS fee of roughly ₦465,500. Officers can also demand a refundable visa bond of $10,000 to $20,000, about ₦13.3 million to ₦26.6 million.

### Is it safe to travel within Nigeria right now?

Safety in Nigeria depends heavily on location, with 23 states under American Level 4 warnings while Lagos, Abuja and much of the south-west see millions of visitors safely each year. Avoid interstate road travel after dark, check your insurer’s exclusions and follow local advice before visiting any state on the Level 4 list.
